source.title: Verifying the Linear Representation Hypothesis: How Interpretable Are Vision SAEs?
source.authors: Teodor Chiaburu; Franz Motzkus; Frank Haußer; F. Biessmann

record.tranche_reason: The study measures interpretability and monosemanticity of vision SAE features and argues that common structural proxies do not establish human-aligned concepts. It does not reproduce toy-model superposition or test capacity competition.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on vision SAE interpretability metrics, which bear on V5's interpretability component. It does not test superposition geometry, feature capacity or importance, LLM feature distributions, or feature stability and completeness. The cited toy-model and other literature results are not rows. The Gemma-scale comparison and random-caption control concern AIS procedure performance, rather than whether SAE features are canonical units.
record.test_reason: The study scores how interpretable vision SAE features are (AIS, MS) and how standard SAE metrics correlate. It does not measure superposition geometry, capacity competition, other causes of polysemanticity, or LLM features. It also does not measure whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units. Interpretability scores with no baseline cannot show any of these. Its LRH discussion and its low-interpretability result are a related but different construct, so they go under fits_no_version, not a test of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also frame the work as challenging the LRH on which SAEs rest. They say vision SAE features remain 'rather opaque' despite high reconstruction, and claim their caption-based AIS matches human judgement (r=0.62, n=14 images, 16 users). They call for ground-truth-anchored SAE design and evaluation.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates vision SAEs and adapts an NLP autointerpretability procedure; it does not reproduce the toy-model intervention or geometry measurements in Toy Models of Superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: AIS and MS vary across SAE architecture, embedder and dataset; the paper also reports layer-dependent values in its DINO/CUB ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Across Vanilla, TopK and MP SAEs on DINO, ViT and SigLIP patch embeddings, Mean AIS stays below 0.5 (0.0226–0.4332). Mean MS is 4e-4–0.106. Connectivity is near 1.0 in nearly all configurations, which the authors read as SAE concepts remaining polysemantic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision SAE features trained on patch embeddings are only weakly human-interpretable despite high reconstruction R2 (>0.89).

fits_no_version.finding: Table 5 (DINO/CUB, Vanilla SAE): SAE features have higher AIS than raw embeddings at every layer (final 0.3493 vs 0.2764) but lower MS (0.0500 vs 0.0602). Interpretability also peaks in intermediate layers, not the final one.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether SAE features are more interpretable than raw neurons depends on the interpretability metric chosen.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 3: LRH structural proxies (sparsity, coherence) and AIS/MS do not correlate as the LRH predicts. Sparsity–Coherence is strongly negative (-0.91), and MS–AIS is uncorrelated (0.23).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary structural properties (sparsity, low coherence) do not track human-aligned interpretability of SAE features.

record.problems: The AIS evaluation relies on patch captions and LLM explanation/simulation, and the authors note that captioning and LLM errors can affect the score, making it unclear how much low AIS reflects SAE concept quality. The human validation used two MP-SAE neurons and 16 valid users; the authors describe the image-level correlation estimate as imprecise given the small sample. AIS uses a limited set of examples per feature.
record.rows_left_out: No additional Table 2 results were left out. Rows are limited to AIS and MS, which directly assess the interpretability or image-level purity of SAE features; other dictionary and reconstruction metrics were not cataloged as measures of V5.

untested.parts: Toy networks, overlapping near-orthogonal feature directions, sparsity-dependent transition, geometry.
Feature importance and capacity determining dedicated vs shared dimensions.
LLM feature distribution across neurons and dictionary recovery in LLMs. Only vision encoders are studied.
Completeness, stability across seeds or settings, and canonicality of SAE features. These are only cited from other work (e.g. Paulo & Belrose), not measured.
One-dimensional vs multi-dimensional features. Only discussed via citations (Engels et al., Bhalla et al.).

record.verdict_notes: Rows were grouped by range (r01–r27 AIS, r28–r54 MS) because the same fix applies to each row in the group. The AIS score depends on the captioner, the grid size (4x4) and the LLM size: Gemma scales give 0.20–0.35 on the same configuration. The authors admit low AIS may not reflect SAE quality alone. The Table 5 raw-neuron comparison would be the relevant baseline if the registry adds an SAE-interpretability version.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, overlapping feature directions, a sparsity-dependent transition, and regular superposition geometry.
Whether feature importance and limited capacity cause some features to get dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemanticity arises from mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
LLM representations and evidence that features spread across neurons or are recovered by dictionaries.

The study evaluates interpretability and monosemanticity-related properties of vision SAE features, but does not test whether features are complete, stable across training or settings, or canonical units of the model.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional subspaces.

rows.subject: Vanilla SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured Mean AIS of SAE features
rows.note: AIS is the mean Pearson correlation between simulated and ground-truth patch activations; the authors describe vision SAE AIS values as low.
rows.check: Mean AIS values from Table 2 measure LLM-simulated human interpretability of vision SAE features. No baseline is given; the raw-neuron baseline exists only in Table 5 for DINO/CUB. V5 names completeness, stability and canonicality, which AIS does not measure. 'Partial' has no reference value to rest on.

relation.reason: Superposition motivates and is discussed alongside the SAE evaluation, but the study's own results do not test any catalog claim version.

tranche.reason: The study measures vision-SAE interpretability and correlations among evaluation metrics, a different construct from V1–V6. Its stated challenge to LRH does not establish a result about dictionary completeness, stability or canonicality.

source_check.notes: All 20 sampled values match Table 2. The authors acknowledge that captioning and explainer/simulator errors prevent attributing low AIS solely to poor SAE-feature interpretability.
